\title{\textbf{The Estimator or the Optimiser?\\
A Walk-Forward Decomposition of Bayesian Methods\\

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=red!4!white,colframe=red!55!black,title=\textbf{Correction notice}]
This paper supersedes an earlier version (March 2025) which reported that Bayesian
optimisation improved the Sharpe ratio by approximately 35\% and reduced maximum
drawdown by approximately 34\%. \textbf{Those results were invalid.} Portfolio
weights were fitted on the full sample and then evaluated on that same sample, so
the reported figures were in-sample fit statistics rather than performance
estimates. The comparison was additionally confounded: the two methods were given
different feasible sets and different search budgets. A full account is given in
Section~\ref{sec:correction} and in \texttt{docs/postmortem.md} in the
accompanying repository. The original code is preserved under \texttt{legacy/}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{abstract}
Comparisons between portfolio construction methods routinely change three things
at once --- how expected returns and covariances are estimated, how weights are
searched for, and what constraints apply --- and then attribute the whole
difference to whichever component the title names. This paper separates them. On
a panel of \nAssets{} US-listed assets sampled weekly, five belief formation rules
(sample moments, Ledoit--Wolf shrinkage, Bayes--Stein, a Normal--Inverse--Wishart
posterior predictive, and Black--Litterman) are crossed with three allocators
(minimum variance, convex maximum-Sharpe, and Gaussian-process Bayesian
optimisation of the identical objective over the identical feasible set). All
\nTrials{} configurations are evaluated by rolling-origin walk-forward over
\oosPeriods{} out-of-sample weeks (\oosStart{} to \oosEnd{}), net of \costBps{}~bps
transaction costs charged on turnover, and tested against the equally weighted
benchmark using the Ledoit--Wolf studentised block bootstrap, stationary-bootstrap
confidence intervals, and the Deflated Sharpe Ratio counting every configuration
tried. Of the \nStrategies{} optimised configurations, \nBeatingBenchmark{}
separated from the 1/N benchmark at the 5\% level. The best configuration reached
a Sharpe of \bestSharpe{} against the benchmark's \benchSharpe{}, a gap of
\bestSharpeGap{} with a bootstrap $p$-value of \bestPValue{}; the benchmark's own
95\% interval alone spans $[\benchCILow{}, \benchCIHigh{}]$. Holding the objective
and the feasible set fixed, replacing convex optimisation with Gaussian-process
search moved mean Sharpe by \optimiserDelta{} while raising mean turnover from
\convexTurnover{} to \gpTurnover{}. In this regime the search method is not where
the performance is, and the sampling variability of a Sharpe ratio estimated on
\oosPeriods{} observations exceeds every effect measured.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Mean--variance portfolio selection \citep{markowitz1952} requires two inputs that
must be estimated: a vector of expected returns $\mu$ and a covariance matrix
$\Sigma$. The optimisation that follows is, given those inputs, a solved problem
--- for the constraint sets used in practice it is a small convex program.

This creates an asymmetry that is easy to lose sight of. Improving the
\emph{optimiser} can at best recover a solution that convex methods already find.
Improving the \emph{estimator} changes what is being solved for. And because
mean--variance optimisation is, in \citeauthor{michaud1989}'s phrase, an
error-maximising procedure --- it loads onto whichever asset's mean was most
overestimated --- estimation error is amplified rather than averaged away.

Despite this, a substantial applied literature reports that some
optimisation technique ``beats mean--variance''. Such comparisons are frequently
uninterpretable, because the compared arms differ in their estimators, their
feasible sets, and the computational effort spent searching, all at once. The
present paper is a deliberately narrow attempt to do the comparison properly, on
one dataset, with the confounds removed:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Holding the objective and the feasible set fixed, how much out-of-sample
performance is attributable to the estimator, and how much to the optimiser?}
\end{quote}

The design is factorial, the evaluation is walk-forward, the feasible set is
shared by construction, and the conclusions are accompanied by hypothesis tests
and confidence intervals rather than point estimates.

An earlier version of this work reported a large advantage for Bayesian
optimisation. That result was an artefact of in-sample evaluation, and correcting
it is a substantial part of what this paper reports;
Section~\ref{sec:correction} treats the error directly, because the mechanism by
which it produced a confidently wrong answer is more instructive than the answer
was.

\section{Literature Review}
\citet{markowitz1952} established the mean--variance framework.
\citet{michaud1989} identified its central practical weakness: optimised
portfolios are extremely sensitive to estimation error in $\mu$, and the
optimiser systematically overweights assets whose returns have been
overestimated. \citet{best1991} quantified this, showing that small perturbations
in estimated means produce large changes in optimal weights.

Two responses dominate. The first shrinks the inputs. \citet{jorion1986} applies
Stein estimation to the mean vector, shrinking toward the return of the global
minimum-variance portfolio with a data-determined intensity.
\citet{ledoit2004} derive an analytically optimal shrinkage of the sample
covariance toward a structured target, with an intensity minimising expected
squared Frobenius error. \citet{black1992} take a different route, treating a
reference portfolio's implied returns as a prior and blending in explicit views.

The second response abandons optimisation altogether. \citet{demiguel2009}
compared fourteen optimised policies against the equally weighted portfolio across
seven datasets and found that none consistently beat it out of sample; the
estimation error introduced by optimisation outweighed the theoretical gains. This
is the benchmark against which any claim of improvement must be measured, and its
omission is a recurring weakness in applied work --- including the earlier version
of this study.

Bayesian optimisation is a separate tradition concerned with optimising expensive
black-box functions \citep{snoek2012, shahriari2016, frazier2018}. It has been
highly successful in hyperparameter tuning, where each evaluation is costly and no
gradient is available. Its application to portfolio weight selection is less
obviously motivated: the Sharpe objective under linear constraints is cheap to
evaluate and smooth. Testing whether it nonetheless helps is one of the two
questions posed here.

Finally, the inference literature: \citet{jobson1981} and \citet{memmel2003}
provide a closed-form test for the equality of two Sharpe ratios,
\citet{ledoit2008} a version robust to the fat tails and autocorrelation of real
returns, \citet{politis1994} a resampling scheme preserving serial dependence, and
\citet{bailey2014} a correction for the selection bias induced by reporting the
best of many backtested configurations.

\section{Theoretical Foundations}
Bayesian Optimization is a probabilistic method used to optimize expensive
black-box functions. At its core, it relies on a Gaussian Process (GP) to model
the unknown function. A GP defines a distribution over functions, characterized by
a mean function \( m(x) \) and a covariance function \( k(x, x') \). Typically,
the mean is assumed to be zero, and the covariance is modeled using kernels such
as the Radial Basis Function (RBF):
\[
k(x, x') = \sigma^2 \exp\left(-\frac{\|x - x'\|^2}{2l^2}\right),
\]
where \( l \) is the length scale and \( \sigma^2 \) is the variance. This kernel
captures the intuition that points closer together in the parameter space will
have similar function values.

The GP provides a predictive distribution for any new point \( x \), delivering
both a mean prediction and an uncertainty measure (variance). This uncertainty
quantification is what makes Bayesian Optimization robust to noisy observations.

The next critical component is the acquisition function, which directs the search
for the optimum. The Expected Improvement (EI) function is defined as:
\[
EI(x) = \mathbb{E}\left[\max\left(0, f(x) - f(x^*)\right)\right],
\]
where \( f(x^*) \) is the current best observation. EI balances the trade-off
between exploring areas with high uncertainty and exploiting regions with a
promising expected value.

\subsection{Derivation of the Expected Improvement (EI) Function}
Let \( f(x) \) be the unknown objective function modeled by a Gaussian Process
with predictive mean \( \mu(x) \) and standard deviation \( \sigma(x) \) at any
point \( x \). Let \( f(x^*) \) be the best observed value so far. The improvement
at \( x \) is defined as:
\[
I(x) = \max\{0, f(x) - f(x^*)\}.
\]
Since \( f(x) \) follows a normal distribution,
\[
f(x) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu(x), \sigma(x)^2),
\]
the expected improvement is given by:
\[
EI(x) = \mathbb{E}[I(x)] = \int_{f(x^*)}^{\infty} \left( f(x) - f(x^*) \right) p(f(x)) \, df(x),
\]
where
\[
p(f(x)) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} \exp\left( -\frac{(f(x) - \mu(x))^2}{2\sigma(x)^2} \right).
\]

A change of variable is performed by letting
\[
z = \frac{f(x) - \mu(x)}{\sigma(x)},
\]
so that
\[
f(x) = \mu(x) + \sigma(x)z \quad \text{and} \quad df(x) = \sigma(x) \, dz.
\]
The lower limit becomes:
\[
z^* = \frac{f(x^*) - \mu(x)}{\sigma(x)}.
\]
Substituting into the integral yields:
\[
EI(x) = \sigma(x) \int_{z^*}^{\infty} \Big[\mu(x) + \sigma(x)z - f(x^*)\Big] \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{z^2}{2} \right) dz.
\]
Defining \( \Delta(x) = \mu(x) - f(x^*) \) simplifies the expression to:
\[
EI(x) = \sigma(x) \left[ \Delta(x) \int_{z^*}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{z^2}{2} \right) dz + \sigma(x) \int_{z^*}^{\infty} z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{z^2}{2} \right) dz \right].
\]
Recognize that:
\[
\int_{z^*}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{z^2}{2} \right) dz = 1 - \Phi(z^*)
\]
and
\[
\int_{z^*}^{\infty} z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{z^2}{2} \right) dz = \phi(z^*),
\]
where \( \Phi(\cdot) \) and \( \phi(\cdot) \) denote the CDF and PDF of the
standard normal distribution, respectively.

By defining
\[
Z = \frac{\Delta(x)}{\sigma(x)} = \frac{\mu(x) - f(x^*)}{\sigma(x)},
\]
the Expected Improvement becomes:
\[
EI(x) = \Delta(x)\Phi(Z) + \sigma(x)\phi(Z).
\]

\subsection{Bayesian optimisation is not Bayesian statistics}
\label{sec:two-bayes}
The derivation above concerns a posterior over an \emph{objective function}, used
to decide where to sample next. It says nothing about a posterior over
\emph{returns}. These are different applications of Bayes' rule to different
objects, and conflating them was the conceptual error underlying the earlier
version of this project, which described itself as Bayesian on the strength of
calling \texttt{gp\_minimize} while estimating $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ with plain
sample moments.

Since estimation error in $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ is the binding constraint in
portfolio choice, and since a Gaussian process over the weight space does nothing
about it, this paper implements both and measures them separately.

\section{The Belief Layer}
Each estimator maps a training window onto a predictive mean and covariance.

\paragraph{Sample moments.} Maximum likelihood; the baseline.

\paragraph{Ledoit--Wolf shrinkage.} $\hat\Sigma = \delta F + (1-\delta)S$, with $F$
imposing the average pairwise correlation on every pair and $\delta$ chosen to
minimise expected squared Frobenius error \citep{ledoit2004}. The
constant-correlation target is preferred to scaled identity because equities share
a dominant market factor.

\paragraph{Bayes--Stein.} Following \citet{jorion1986}, the mean is shrunk toward
$\mu_{\text{GMV}}$, the expected return of the global minimum-variance portfolio:
\[
\hat\mu_{BS} = (1-w)\hat\mu + w\,\mu_{\text{GMV}}\mathbf{1},
\qquad w = \frac{\lambda}{T+\lambda},
\qquad \lambda = \frac{N+2}{(\hat\mu - \mu_{\text{GMV}}\mathbf{1})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\hat\mu - \mu_{\text{GMV}}\mathbf{1})}.
\]
The covariance is inflated to reflect that $\mu$ is estimated rather than known.

\paragraph{Normal--Inverse--Wishart posterior predictive.} A conjugate prior
$\mu \mid \Sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \Sigma/\kappa_0)$,
$\Sigma \sim \mathcal{W}^{-1}(\Psi_0, \nu_0)$, conditioned on the training window.
The predictive distribution of the next return is multivariate-$t$ with
$\nu_n - N + 1$ degrees of freedom and covariance
\[
\frac{\Psi_n (\kappa_n + 1)}{\kappa_n (\nu_n - N - 1)},
\]
strictly wider than the plug-in estimate. The prior is centred on a common mean
across assets, encoding ``absent evidence, assets earn the same''.

\paragraph{Black--Litterman.} Reverse-optimisation of a reference portfolio gives
$\Pi = \delta \Sigma w_{\text{ref}}$ as the prior; a cross-sectional momentum view
is blended in with uncertainty proportional to the view's own variance
\citep{black1992}. The reference portfolio is equal-weight, since this panel
carries no market capitalisations --- an approximation that is flagged rather than
concealed.

\section{The Search Layer}
All allocators optimise over the same set
\[
\mathcal{W} = \Big\{ w \in \mathbb{R}^{N} : \textstyle\sum_i w_i = 1,\; 0 \le w_i \le \maxWeight \Big\}.
\]
This is enforced in code by a single constraint object passed to every allocator,
whose output is checked against it. Long-only with a per-asset cap reflects a
realistic mandate and regularises the extreme positions that unconstrained
mean--variance produces on estimated inputs.

\paragraph{Equal weight (1/N).} Ignores the belief entirely \citep{demiguel2009}.

\paragraph{Minimum variance.} Uses $\Sigma$, ignores $\mu$. A diagnostic: if it
wins, the $\mu$ estimates carry no exploitable signal.

\paragraph{Convex.} Multi-start sequential least-squares maximisation of the
Sharpe ratio.

\paragraph{Gaussian-process Bayesian optimisation.} \texttt{gp\_minimize} with
Expected Improvement and a budget of \gpBudget{} evaluations, searching in
unconstrained logit space with a softmax-then-projection map onto $\mathcal{W}$.
Sampling in $[0,1]^N$ and normalising afterwards --- the earlier approach --- is
not a uniform parameterisation of the simplex and biases the search toward its
interior.

Both optimisers expose a search budget, so effort can be equalised. This matters:
on a fixed, already-observed objective the more thorough search always wins, which
is precisely how the earlier version manufactured its result.

\section{Experimental Design}
Weekly adjusted closes for \nAssets{} US-listed assets, differenced to total
returns. Weights held over period $t$ depend only on returns strictly before $t$:
a \trainWindow{}-week rolling training window, rebalancing every
\rebalanceEvery{} weeks, yielding \oosPeriods{} out-of-sample observations from
\oosStart{} to \oosEnd{}. Between rebalances the portfolio is held rather than
reset, so weights drift and turnover is measured against drifted holdings.
Transaction costs of \costBps{}~bps are charged on traded notional, once, in the
period the trade occurs.

Causality is not merely asserted. The accompanying test suite corrupts all returns
after a cutoff date and asserts that every weight decided before it is bitwise
unchanged; a violation anywhere in the estimator or allocator stack would fail it.

Significance is assessed with the \citet{memmel2003} closed-form test, the
\citet{ledoit2008} studentised circular block bootstrap (the headline test, robust
to fat tails and serial dependence), \citet{politis1994} stationary-bootstrap
confidence intervals, and the \citet{bailey2014} Deflated Sharpe Ratio computed
over all \nTrials{} configurations --- including those that lost.

\section{The Correction}
\label{sec:correction}
The March 2025 version of this study reported a 35\% Sharpe improvement and a 34\%
drawdown reduction for Bayesian optimisation. The mechanism was as follows.
Expected returns and covariances were computed over the entire 2012--2023 history;
both optimisers maximised the Sharpe ratio implied by those full-sample moments;
and performance was then evaluated on the same return series used to fit the
weights. No train/test split existed anywhere in the analysis. The notebook that
produced the published figures did not call an optimiser at all --- it applied two
hardcoded weight vectors, copied from an earlier run, to the full in-sample series.

Two features made a positive result close to certain, independent of whether the
method had any merit. First, on a fixed and already-observed objective, a
50-evaluation global search lands nearer the in-sample optimum than a single
convex solve; the reported gap measured search thoroughness, and a higher
in-sample score reflects \emph{more} overfitting, not more robustness. Second, the
two arms were given different feasible sets --- the convex arm could short, the
Bayesian arm could not --- so the comparison confounded method with constraint.

Instructively, the earlier report's limitations section listed six caveats, every
one of them a generic property of Gaussian processes --- among them kernel
sensitivity, cubic scaling, stationarity assumptions and convergence to local
optima --- and not one of them the absence of an out-of-sample split. The closest
it came was a final item on ``dependence on historical data'', which warned that
results might not transfer if future conditions diverged from the past. Even that
framing presumes the backtest had measured something about the past that could
transfer. It had not: it had measured the fit of the weights to the very returns
they were chosen on. A limitations section assembled from generic properties of a
technique, rather than from an attack on one's own design, produces the appearance
of rigour without its substance.

\section{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}
\begin{enumerate}[noitemsep]
  \item \textbf{Universe size and selection.} \nAssets{} assets is small, and they
  were not chosen by a stated prior rule. With $N = \nAssets{}$ and
  $T = \trainWindow{}$ the ratio $N/T$ is mild --- precisely the regime in which
  shrinkage estimators have least to offer. This study is therefore a weak test of
  the estimators it compares, and a wider universe is the single most valuable
  extension.
  \item \textbf{Survivorship.} All assets were liquid and listed throughout.
  \item \textbf{One market regime.} The out-of-sample window is dominated by a US
  equity bull market with two sharp drawdowns. It is one path, not a distribution
  over paths.
  \item \textbf{Cost model.} Proportional costs only: no market impact, no spread
  modelling, no capacity constraint. Adequate at these turnover levels, not at
  higher frequencies.
  \item \textbf{View specification.} The Black--Litterman momentum view uses a
  26-week lookback and 50\% damping. Neither was tuned --- deliberately, since
  tuning on this panel would reintroduce the selection bias the Deflated Sharpe
  Ratio exists to penalise --- but neither is derived from first principles.
  \item \textbf{Single asset class.} Six equities and one Treasury ETF.
  \item \textbf{Statistical power.} With \oosPeriods{} observations, only large
  Sharpe differences are detectable. A null result here is an absence of evidence,
  not evidence of exact equality.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Reproducibility}
All figures, tables and inline numbers in this document are generated from
\texttt{results/}, which is produced by \texttt{experiments/run\_backtest.py}. No
value is transcribed by hand --- the failure mode that produced the original
error. The price panel is committed to the repository, the test suite includes a
look-ahead poison test, and the full run is exercised in continuous integration.
